cells.value: The agent works through a series of tool calls, deciding what to do next based on the result of each action. It uses tools to search code, edit files, and run the terminal, then reads each result before its next step. A stop hook is called when the agent loop ends and can optionally auto-submit a follow-up user message to keep iterating.

There is no limit on the number of tool calls Agent can make during a task. Stop-hook auto follow-ups have a default limit of 5 per script, configurable via loop_limit; setting loop_limit to null removes the cap. The same limit applies to subagentStop follow-ups.

cells.value: Agent tools include file editing, codebase search, terminal execution, and more. First-party tools cover reading files, editing files, running terminal commands, searching the web, and more. Hook matchers filter by tool type, with values including Shell, Read, Write, Grep, Delete, Task, and MCP tools in the MCP:<tool_name> format.

cells.value: Cursor runs shell commands directly in your terminal; Run Mode controls when commands run, when Cursor asks, and when terminal commands enter the sandbox. By default Cursor uses the first terminal profile available and requires your approval before executing any terminal command. The LocalAgentOptions cwd is the primary working directory for the default shell.

cells.value: The built-in ToolCall union covers shell, edit, read, write, glob, grep, ls, semSearch, mcp, task, and others. A search tool can search for files by name, read directory structures, and find exact keywords or patterns within files. afterFileEdit fires after the Agent edits a file.

cells.value: A Web tool generates search queries and performs web searches. For the web fetch tool, without an allowlist entry each fetch prompts for approval, and domains added to allow are auto-approved. An Auto-Accept Web Search permission lets the agent run web searches without pausing for approval each time; it is off by default.

Cloud Agents let you select the context window size; a larger window can increase token usage and costs. A subagent model string such as claude-opus-5[context=300k] sets the context window to 300k tokens. On request-based plans, Max Mode enables larger context windows.
cells.limitation: Automations use each model's maximum supported context window because they run as cloud agents. There is no context-window toggle.

cells.value: When the context window gets close to full, Cursor compresses older parts of the conversation into a summary to leave more room for new conversation. The preCompact hook is called before compaction and is observational: it cannot block or modify the compaction behavior.

cells.value: /summarize summarizes the conversation to reduce context and frees up space in the context window; /compress is an alias. A changelog entry says /summarize was renamed from /compress, and /compact and /compress remain as aliases that execute directly.

Adding sensitive paths to .cursorignore keeps them out of the agent's context. beforeReadFile is called before Agent reads a file and can block sensitive files from being sent to the model. The dirs option adds workspace folders for multi-root setups, so rules, skills, and workspace context load from every path.

Commenting @cursor remember [fact] on a PR makes Bugbot save a learned rule and apply it to future reviews. Conversation search lets Agent query past conversations.

Cloud agents read AGENTS.md files. The CLI agent supports the same rules system as the editor; rules in .cursor/rules are automatically loaded and applied based on their configuration. Bugbot reviews are guided by project .cursor/BUGBOT.md files.

The closest applicable APPROVAL_POLICY.md has the highest priority for files under its directory; ancestor policies still apply unless they conflict.

Project rules live in .cursor/rules as .mdc files and are scoped using path patterns, invoked manually, or included based on relevance. The Apply to Specific Files rule type only applies for files matching a pattern (e.g., *.tsx). A paths field on a skill accepts a list or comma-separated string of glob patterns.

cells.value: Terminal commands need approval by default. Run Modes, chosen in the desktop app under Settings > Agents > Approvals & Execution, range from a simple allowlist to the Auto-review classifier. The CLI approvalMode field takes allowlist, auto-review or unrestricted.

permissions.allow, permissions.deny and --force control what runs without prompts. mcpAllowlist lists MCP tools that can run without approval, and Cursor asks for approval before using MCP tools by default. Users can set the agent to always ask before reading files, editing files, running terminal commands, or making network requests.

Read permissions control read access to files and directories and support glob patterns. .cursorignore in the project root blocks listed files from Agent, codebase search, and @ mentions, to block agent read and context for secrets and regulated trees.
cells.limitation: Terminal commands and MCP tools run outside of Cursor's file access controls, so they may still be able to read ignored files.

cells.value: Shell permissions control access to shell commands; the commandBase is the first token in the command line, with glob patterns and an optional command:args syntax. terminalAllowlist lists terminal commands that can run without approval (when set, it overrides the in-app terminal allowlist); each entry is matched against the full command string.
cells.limitation: Allowlists and autoRun instructions are best-effort convenience. They are not a security guarantee.

cells.value: When Workspace Trust is enabled, Cursor prompts users to choose between normal or restricted mode for new workspaces; the WorkspaceTrustEnabled policy controls whether it is enabled. A July 20, 2026 changelog entry says passing --trust in an interactive session trusts the workspace up front, skips the trust dialog and records the same saved trust decision.
cells.limitation: Workspace trust is disabled by default; restricted mode breaks AI features. E-cursor-00317 says --trust trusts without prompting in headless mode only; E-cursor-00145 says it now works in interactive sessions too.

cells.value: Run Everything mode runs every tool call automatically ('You accept the risk and want zero prompts'). In the CLI, -f/--force force-allows commands unless explicitly denied. Browser tools have an Auto-run approval mode that executes all browser actions without approval.

In Auto-review mode, allowlisted calls run immediately, other shell commands run in the sandbox when possible, and calls that do not use the sandbox go to the Auto-review classifier. The autoRun permissions field holds natural-language guidance for the classifier; SDK local.autoReview: true routes local tool calls through it.

Auto-review reads permissions.json from two locations. When a Cursor policy is specified through device management solutions, its value overrides the corresponding Cursor setting on users' devices. Cursor resolves the effective MCP allowlist in an ordered sequence.

cells.value: In Auto-review mode, other shell commands run in the sandbox when possible. Command execution sandbox settings are configured with /sandbox or --sandbox <mode> (enabled or disabled) and persist across sessions. Cursor-hosted cloud runs use an isolated VM with the repo cloned in. Agents run on the local machine by default.

When sandboxed, writes are limited to the working directory, temp directories and paths allowed in sandbox.json; reads are not restricted to the workspace. Sandbox type workspace_readwrite (default) gives read/write access in the workspace. Enterprise teams can prevent agents from modifying the .cursor directory.
cells.limitation: Local agents run with local.sandboxOptions.enabled: false by default; the agent can read and write the working directory, execute shell commands, and reach the network without restriction.

cells.value: Network egress controls restrict outbound traffic to a default set plus an allowlist, or to the allowlist only; enterprise admins can lock the policy org-wide. In the sandbox, --network enables network access (default: false). Cloud Agent network settings apply to Cursor-hosted Cloud Agents.
cells.limitation: Network settings apply to Cursor-hosted Cloud Agents. Local agents run with local.sandboxOptions.enabled: false by default and can reach the network without restriction.

cells.value: On macOS, Cursor uses Seatbelt through sandbox-exec; a generated sandbox profile limits file access, network access, and other process behavior for the full subprocess tree. When the sandbox is enabled, the SDK constrains every shell tool call and shell-spawned process. Cursor injects environment variables into every sandboxed child process.

cells.value: If a sandboxed command fails on a sandbox restriction, such as a permission error, the agent can rerun it outside the sandbox, and the classifier reviews that rerun. Some commands need full system access and bypass the sandbox; Cursor indicates when a command runs outside the sandbox and asks for approval. Sandbox type insecure_none disables the sandbox entirely.

cells.value: Hooks observe, control or extend the agent loop at lifecycle events, in three categories based on what triggers them. Supported hooks on cloud agents include preToolUse, beforeShellExecution and afterFileEdit, plus beforeSubmitPrompt, subagentStart / subagentStop and preCompact. Worker hooks include sessionStart and sessionEnd when a session claims and releases the machine.
Hooks support two execution types: command-based (default) and prompt-based (LLM-evaluated). Cloud agents run command-based hooks from .cursor/hooks.json in the repository.
cells.limitation: On self-hosted workers, only command-based hooks run; prompt-based hooks do not run. The SDK docs say hooks are file-based only, with no programmatic hook callback.

cells.value: Command hooks receive JSON input via stdin. All hooks receive a base set of fields in addition to their hook-specific fields, including conversation_id (stable ID of the conversation across many turns). On a claim, sessionStart input also lists the run's repositories via repo_urls and repos.

cells.value: Exit code 0 means the hook succeeded and its JSON output is used; exit code 2 blocks the action, equivalent to returning permission: deny. For permission hooks, invalid JSON or a response that does not match the hook's schema blocks the action. The nested permissionDecision and updatedInput map to permission and updated_input. failClosed can be set for critical hooks.

A matcher is a regex string that filters when a hook runs; an empty string or * matches everything. For beforeShellExecution it runs against the shell command string; for preToolUse / postToolUse / postToolUseFailure it filters by tool type (values include Shell, Read, Write, Grep, Delete, Task, and MCP:<tool_name>); for subagentStart it runs against the subagent type.

Hook events carry an optional cursor.plugin.name when the hook came from a plugin. Cursor can also load hooks configured for Claude Code.

The Cursor editor and agent can be deployed to workstations with policies enforced through MDM, and ~/.cursor/permissions.json can be distributed through MDM to set the per-user MCP auto-run allowlist from a managed file. cells.value: Custom subagents are markdown files added to .cursor/agents/; plugin agents are markdown files in agents/. The model field in a subagent's YAML frontmatter can be set to a specific model ID; custom subagents default to inherit, which uses the parent agent's model. In the cloud API each custom subagent entry requires name, description and prompt, plus an optional model.

The SDK tools option allowlists the built-in tools offered to the model, and disallowed_tools removes tools and keeps the rest. In a subagent definition, readonly: true (default false) runs the subagent with restricted write permissions (no file edits, no state-changing shell commands). cells.value: A subagent's model field takes inherit (the default) or a specific model ID. Custom subagents default to inherit, using the parent agent's model, unless the model field in the YAML frontmatter sets one. Cloud Agent API customSubagents entries also take an optional model.

Appending square brackets to a model ID sets per-model options such as speed, reasoning effort and context window, written as id=value pairs. For example, claude-opus-5[effort=high] sets reasoning effort to high.

Since Cursor 2.5, subagents can launch child subagents within a nesting limit, forming a tree of coordinated work. The main agent and its direct subagents can launch subagents. The Python SDK docs state the same rule.

Built-in subagents select their model automatically based on the subtask; the Explore subagent runs in its own context window with a faster model. Custom subagent names cannot collide with built-ins (explore, debug, shell, computerUse, etc.).

Official plugins install with one click from Customize via the Cursor Marketplace, which distributes plugins as Git repositories. Skills from a GitHub repository are packaged in a plugin and published through a marketplace. `--plugin-dir <path>` loads a local plugin directory (can be specified multiple times).

cells.value: MCP lets you connect external tools and data sources to Cursor. Cursor automatically uses MCP tools listed under Available Tools when relevant, including in Plan Mode. The CLI detects and respects your `mcp.json`, enabling the same MCP servers and tools as the editor. Instructions and catalog from connected MCP servers count toward context.

Custom MCP servers for cloud agents can use HTTP or stdio transport. Local servers are configured with `command` and `args`. MCP servers can be written in any language that can print to `stdout` or serve an HTTP endpoint. The Python SDK HTTP server config has `type: Literal["http", "sse"]`, default "http".
cells.limitation: For cloud-agent custom MCP servers, "SSE and `mcp-remote` are not supported" (E-cursor-02121), while the Python SDK config type accepts "http" or "sse" (E-cursor-01214); the quotes do not reconcile the two.

cells.value: MCP servers are defined in a project-level or user-level `.cursor/mcp.json`; `agent mcp login` uses servers in `.cursor/mcp.json` or `~/.cursor/mcp.json`. For cloud agents, personal servers are added through the MCP dropdown in cursor.com/agents and team admins configure shared servers under Dashboard -> Plugins & MCPs. The cloud agent API accepts inline MCP server definitions (maximum 50).

Remote servers support `headers` or OAuth `auth`; stdio servers can receive `env`. Cloud agents support OAuth for MCP servers that need it, per-user, including for team-shared servers. For HTTP servers in the cloud, `headers` and `auth` are handled by Cursor's backend and sensitive fields are redacted before the VM sees them. `agent mcp login <identifier>` authenticates with a configured server.

Hook matchers address MCP tools as `MCP:<tool_name>`.

Each subagent execution returns an agent ID to resume it with full context preserved.

Prepending `&` to a CLI message pushes the conversation to a Cloud Agent, which can be picked up on web or mobile at cursor.com/agents. cells.value: Setting is_background: true (default false) runs a subagent in the background without blocking the parent. Background agents are coding agents that typically run for a very long time, moving a task from the local device to the cloud. A background subagent's result returns to the parent as a follow-up turn on the same run (local agents only).

Automations run cloud agents in the background on a schedule or in response to events. Timer subscriptions are a one-off reminder after a delay or a recurring cron schedule. The built-in `/loop` skill runs a prompt or skill on a recurring or variable interval; if you don't specify a fixed interval, the agent chooses when to wake.

The Cloud Agent API can create a Cloud Agent and immediately enqueue its initial run. Runs are listed as a Cloud machine, a Team Pool, or one of My Machines, and agents work in full development environments: they install dependencies, run tests, and verify their changes. Cloud Agents auto-run terminal commands so they can iterate on tests without stopping for approval on every step.

Agents keep working in the cloud whether or not your device stays connected. My Machines lets a specific user run Cloud Agent tool calls on a machine they already use: a laptop, devbox, or remote VM.

cells.value: Automations run cloud agents in response to events from GitHub, GitLab, Slack, webhooks, Linear, and more. Commenting `@cursor` on a GitHub PR or issue, or a Bitbucket PR, kicks off an agent. An agent can subscribe to an event source, end its turn, and wake on a matching event. The PR pushed / updated trigger runs an agent when new commits are pushed to an existing PR.

Subagents are specialized AI assistants that Cursor's agent can delegate tasks to; each operates in its own context window and returns its result to the parent agent. `/in-cloud` hands a task to a cloud subagent, so long-running work runs on its own VM and branch. In a Project, a coordinator agent plans the work and delegates it to other agents.

cells.value: Cursor CLI lets you interact with AI agents from your terminal to write, review, and modify code. With no command specified, Cursor Agent starts in interactive agent mode. In the CLI, pressing Enter while the agent works steers the active run at a safe boundary, and pressing Enter again interrupts the turn. Shell Mode runs shell commands directly from the CLI.

cells.value: `-p`/`--print` prints responses to the console for scripts or non-interactive use and has access to all tools, including write and shell. Combined with `--print`, `--output-format` offers `json` and `stream-json` (structured) or `text`. Print mode suits scripts, CI pipelines, or automation; API key authentication is for automation, scripts, or CI environments.

Cursor's agent runs in IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm and other JetBrains IDEs through the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). `agent acp` runs Cursor CLI as an ACP server over stdio with JSON-RPC messaging. The editor offers the classic IDE with VS Code extensions. `/open` opens the repository's Git root in Cursor; `/cursor` is an alias.

The Agents Window is Cursor's agent-first interface, a unified workspace across repos and environments including local, cloud and remote SSH. In the desktop application, go to Settings > Agents > Approvals & Execution.

cells.value: An API call can create a Cloud Agent and immediately enqueue its initial run; the response returns the durable agent and the initial run. `Agent.create()` takes either `local` or `cloud` to pick a runtime, and a local runtime runs the agent loop inline in your Node process. `agent acp` runs Cursor CLI as an ACP server over stdio with JSON-RPC messaging.

cells.value: Mention @cursor in Slack with a prompt and Cursor tries to detect a repository, model, base branch or named cloud agent environment from your message. Commenting @cursor on a GitHub PR or issue, or on a Bitbucket PR, kicks off an agent. In Microsoft Teams, mentioning @Cursor automatically picks the right repository, model, base branch or environment.

In chat, the model picker dropdown at the top of the chat input switches models (Cmd / cycles through them), and a default can be set in Cursor Settings > Models. In the CLI, the /model slash command selects a model. The picker, including Auto, applies to the parent agent; a subagent can run a different model.

Cloud Agent API: when the model selection is omitted, Cursor resolves the user default model, then the team default, then a system default. Slack: @Cursor [options] [prompt] sets the model, among other options, for a run. Linear: a Default Model setting (Cursor Dashboard) is the AI model for Cloud Agents. Python SDK: ModelSelection.params passes per-model options such as reasoning effort.

Cursor Router is the model routing system behind Auto: simple requests go to fast, efficient models while complex work goes to the most capable ones. Auto selects models that balance intelligence, cost and reliability. Separately, a Fable request that trips a security guardrail is routed to Claude Opus automatically.
cells.limitation: On Teams and Enterprise plans, Cursor Router picks the model for each Auto request based on your optimization mode (E-cursor-01002).

cells.value: You can add your own API key for a supported provider under Models. For AWS Bedrock, the recommended setup is an IAM role granting Cursor permission to invoke Bedrock models on your behalf. The Enterprise plan can disable users from using their own API keys (BYOK).
cells.limitation: Own keys are for 'a supported provider' (E-cursor-00053); US data residency is not supported for BYOK (E-cursor-00765).

cells.value: The CLI models command lists the models available for the account, and the List Models API endpoint returns model IDs with the parameters and variants each model accepts. Some models in Cursor may be unavailable in certain regions, and Enterprise teams can opt in to new models for their organization.

Levels are per model. Grok 4.5 has high (default), medium and low. Grok 4.6 has xhigh, high (default), medium and low. Muse Spark 1.3 has six levels, from minimal to max, with high as the default. Composer has no effort levels.

Effort is set through per-model parameters: the Cloud Agent API model.params array (id and value items, such as reasoning effort or context window size), the SDK's ModelSelection.params, or square-bracket id=value options appended to a model ID.
cells.limitation: On Cursor Start, Grok 4.5 is fixed at medium effort in non-fast mode. You cannot change the effort level or enable Fast mode on that plan (E-cursor-01496).

cells.value: Available model parameter options depend on the model. Each model entry in the API response lists the concrete id+params combinations it accepts. Grok 4.6 supports xhigh, high (default), medium and low; Muse Spark 1.3 has six levels, from minimal to max, with high as the default.

The CLI setting display.showThinkingBlocks renders model thinking blocks when available. The cloud-agent run stream emits a thinking event carrying thinking text deltas. Grok 4.5 supports three effort levels: high (the default), medium, and low.
cells.limitation: `thinking` events are suppressed in print mode and will not appear in any output format (E-cursor-01829); the cloud-agent run stream emits them (E-cursor-01951).

cells.value: The CLI --mode flag takes plan or ask, with agent as the default. Debug Mode has the agent generate hypotheses, add log statements and use runtime information before a targeted fix. Design Mode lets users direct agents by clicking an element, drawing on the page or describing a change by voice. A skill can be used as a Custom Mode.

The CLI --mode flag sets plan or ask (agent is the default). /plan switches to Plan mode in the CLI. Shift+Tab from the chat input rotates to Plan Mode. The mode picker dropdown in Agent switches modes.

Plan Mode researches the codebase, asks clarifying questions and generates a reviewable plan the user can edit before building. In the CLI it is entered via Shift+Tab, /plan, --plan or --mode=plan. Over ACP, cursor/create_plan requests plan approval and blocks until the client accepts or rejects the plan.
cells.limitation: File editing is listed as "Yes (after you approve the plan)" (E-cursor-03980); no cited quote labels Plan mode read-only.

cells.value: The CLI /run-everything [on|off|status] toggles Run Everything, with /auto-run as an alias. Auto-approval for terminal commands can be enabled, with documented risks including destructive commands and prompt injection. --yolo gives fully autonomous runs that auto-approve across trust, MCP, and command approvals.

Ask mode is a read-only mode: Agent answers questions and explores code without making any edits. In the CLI it is entered with /ask or --mode=ask. A subagent with readonly: true runs with restricted write permissions (no file edits, no state-changing shell commands).

Agent is the default mode (no --mode value needed in the CLI; the SDK AgentOptions mode defaults to agent). On follow-up SDK sends, omitting mode keeps the conversation's current mode; passing mode switches for that run only. Each mode uses its own context, so switching modes starts a fresh context window.

`/about` shows CLI version, system and account info and also copies it to the clipboard. The CLI changelog page says to run `agent --version` to check your installed version. `SdkBridgeControlService.GetVersion` can be called to gate on `bridge_version`, `protocol_version` or `capabilities` at runtime.

cells.value: Update channels include Stable (default, recommended for most users) and Early Access (pre-release builds with the latest features, may be less stable). The CLI configuration has a `channel` string field: the release channel used for CLI updates.

Cursor CLI will try to auto-update by default; `/update` updates Cursor Agent to the latest version. The UpdateMode MDM policy (`update.mode`) controls automatic update behavior; set it to 'none' to disable updates. On Linux, the apt and yum packages provide automatic updates.

The CLI changelog page lists the latest features, improvements and fixes shipping to Cursor CLI. A separate SDK changelog covers the latest features, improvements and fixes for `@cursor/sdk` on npm and `cursor-sdk` on PyPI.

cells.value: Cursor is based upon the VS Code codebase. It is regularly rebased onto the latest VS Code version, and often uses slightly older VS Code versions for stability.

SDK runs follow the same pricing, request pools, and Privacy Mode rules as the IDE and Cloud Agents. Cursor ACP uses the same usage-based pricing as the Cursor subscription. Notion usage is billed through the existing account. Service account API keys bill to the owning team; user API keys bill to that user's plan.

env.type cloud uses Cursor-hosted VMs; pool and machine route to the customer's own workers. Security Agents run on Cloud Agents. Pools do not move the agent loop out of Cursor's cloud; the worker executes tool calls in the customer's infrastructure.
cells.limitation: The exception is a team's Security Reviewer: when a pull request event triggers it, the review runs on Cursor-managed hosting instead of a Cloud Agent (E-cursor-03875).

cells.value: The Cursor SDK launches agents with the same harness, runtime, and models that power Cursor. The CLI is the same agent as the editor's with a different interface. The Notion integration is built on the Cursor SDK. The Python SDK scripts the same agent that runs in the IDE, CLI, and web app.

From a local agent session you can hand off work to a cloud subagent that runs on its own VM and branch; /in-cloud does this from the Agents Window. The CLI changelog lists typing & to transfer the live conversation to a cloud agent.
target.openAsCursorGithubApp opens the pull request as the Cursor GitHub App instead of as the user. Cursor says it tunes its harness to each frontier model it supports.

cells.value: The Spending dashboard shows request-level cost and pool details. The context ring next to the prompt input shows how full the window is; its breakdown tray shows total tokens used by category. `getUsage` fetches billed token usage and dollar cost for the agent, and an API endpoint retrieves token usage for an agent broken down per run.

You'll be asked to set a spend limit when you first start using Cloud Agents. Team limits are pooled usage plus admin-only controls. A group's settings page includes Spend Limit Overrides. When the Other Models allowance runs out on a Teams or Enterprise plan, own-key requests keep working if on-demand usage is enabled and stop until the next billing cycle if it is off.

cells.value: OpenTelemetry Export streams usage metrics and logs to your observability stack over OTLP. Everything is on by default for a new destination except `conversation_content`, and individual families can be turned off in Team Settings. All metrics are monotonic delta sums. Starting a worker with `--management-addr` exposes `GET /metrics`, `/healthz` and `/readyz`.

cells.value: `/logs` shows the debug log path and copies it to the clipboard. `--data-dir <path>` on the worker command sets the base directory for logs, artifacts and recording data. Cloud Agents include a built-in Cursor Cloud MCP for run diagnostics, including transcripts, run events, environment details and setup logs.

The built-in `/statusline` skill configures the Cursor CLI status line. `display.showStatusLineRunningTime` shows elapsed running time in the status line. A context ring next to the prompt input shows how full the window is at a glance; clicking it opens a breakdown tray of total tokens used by category.
